beats.narration: Permissions decide what the agent may do. This section decides what it knows, and makes that knowledge survive between sessions. Four mechanisms, each with a different loading behavior and a different cost: a file that always loads, rules that load where they apply, hooks that fire no matter what the model thinks, and subagents that keep their mess out of your context.

items.text: rules files — load where they apply
hooks — fire regardless of the model

beats.narration: CLAUDE dot M D is the file Claude Code reads at the start of every session, prepended before your first message. Whatever lives there, testing commands, framework conventions, forbidden paths, is present from prompt one, every time. The init command generates a starter version. Validate it, then keep refining. And know the one failure mode that matters: size. Every line you add dilutes every other line, because a bigger file makes each instruction a smaller fraction of what loads. Keep it to constraints that change behavior. Everything else belongs elsewhere, and that's what the next three mechanisms are for.

elements.text: session start → CLAUDE.md → your first prompt

the failure mode is SIZE:
every line dilutes every other line

beats.narration: For guidance that only matters in one part of the codebase, rules files. They live in the claude rules directory, and a paths glob in their frontmatter scopes them: the rule enters context only when Claude works on matching files. A transaction-boundary rule for the database module loads when database files are touched, and never clutters anything else. One subtlety worth remembering: the scoping comes from the frontmatter, not from where the file sits. A rules file without a paths field loads unconditionally, just like CLAUDE dot M D, no matter how neatly you organized it into subdirectories. So the split is: universal constraints in CLAUDE dot M D, path-specific guidance in scoped rules.

elements.code:
# .claude/rules/database.md
---
paths:
  - "src/db/**/*.sql"
---
All SQL must use explicit transactions.

elements.text:
loads ONLY when
matching files
are touched

⚠ scoping = frontmatter, not folder;
no paths field → loads like CLAUDE.md

beats.narration: Now the difference between a convention and a guardrail. Write run prettier after every edit into CLAUDE dot M D, and the agent follows it most of the time. Wire it as a hook, and it happens every time, because hooks fire independently of what the model decides. Each hook binds a lifecycle event, an optional matcher, and a command. The two you'll use most: pre tool use runs before a tool call, and can block it, exit code two, with the reason on standard error becoming feedback the agent sees. That's enforcement, not hope. Post tool use runs after: formatters, test triggers, audit logs. There are more events, session start and end, prompt submission, notifications, but the principle is the one to keep: rules the project cannot afford to lose belong in hooks, not in prose.

elements.text:
PreToolUse — can BLOCK
(exit 2 + stderr → agent feedback)
can't afford to lose it? → hook, not prose

beats.narration: Here's dilution in the wild. A team's CLAUDE dot M D grew for two months. Every addition individually reasonable. Eight hundred forty-seven lines: framework preferences, style guide, dependency rules... and a historical decisions log spanning three hundred lines. Line three forty-seven said: do not modify the legacy tokens directory. The user even repeated it in the prompt. The agent read the auth module, and edited legacy tokens anyway. The rule was there. The agent had it. But eight hundred forty-six other lines had shrunk its weight until it stopped landing. The audit that follows is the fix: keep session-critical rules, move path-specific ones into scoped rules files, move history into reference docs. And the one rule you absolutely cannot afford to dilute? That's not a rule. That's a hook.

elements.code:
CLAUDE.md: 847 lines
  style guide ......... 120 lines
  decisions log ....... 340 lines (?!)
  line 347: "do not modify /legacy/tokens/"

elements.text:
agent edits /legacy/tokens/ anyway —
the rule was there, its WEIGHT was gone
audit: critical stays · path-specific → rules · history → docs

beats.narration: Last mechanism: subagents, the same isolation pattern you know from module two, built in. A subagent runs a task in its own context and returns only the output. Perfect for exploration that would bloat your session. But mind what each one loads. The built-in explore and plan subagents skip CLAUDE dot M D to stay fast, so your project rules are not in their heads. The general-purpose subagent loads them. And custom subagents don't see your skills unless the frontmatter lists them explicitly. When project constraints must hold, pick the subagent that actually carries them.
